content:
Sudden joint swelling is most often caused by an injury, gout, pseudogout or a flare of arthritis. A joint that is suddenly hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially with fever or feeling unwell, could be an infection called septic arthritis, which is an emergency. Get any unexplained swollen joint checked the same day by NHS 111 or your GP.

Common causes

Injury

A sprain, ligament tear, cartilage tear or fracture can cause swelling within hours. Rapid swelling after a twisting injury may mean bleeding into the joint and should be assessed.

Gout

Crystals of uric acid cause sudden severe pain and swelling, often in the big toe, ankle or knee, frequently starting at night.

Pseudogout (CPPD)

Calcium crystals cause similar attacks, often in the knee or wrist, mainly in older adults.

Septic arthritis

A bacterial infection inside the joint. It usually affects one joint, which is hot, red, swollen and very painful, often with fever. It can damage the joint within days and needs emergency hospital treatment. People with joint replacements, diabetes, weakened immune systems or existing arthritis are at higher risk.

Inflammatory arthritis

Rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and other conditions can cause swelling, often in several joints, with stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes in the morning.

Reactive arthritis

Swelling a few weeks after a bowel or sexually transmitted infection.

Osteoarthritis flare

Knees in particular can swell during a flare, usually after more activity.

Bursitis

Swelling of a fluid-filled sac, such as in front of the knee or behind the elbow. It can become infected.

Other causes

Lyme disease after a tick bite, viral infections and blood disorders are less common causes.

What to do while you wait to be seen

For swelling after a minor injury, if you can still bear weight and there are no warning signs:

  • rest the joint for a day or two
  • use an ice pack wrapped in a towel for up to 20 minutes every few hours
  • raise the joint above heart level when you can
  • use a pharmacist-recommended painkiller or gel
  • avoid heat in the first two days

Gradually start gentle movement as pain allows.

When to see your GP

See your GP if:

  • swelling has not improved after a few days
  • swelling keeps coming back
  • several joints are swollen
  • you have morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes
  • you also have rashes, eye problems, bowel symptoms or psoriasis

NICE recommends urgent referral to a rheumatologist for persistent joint swelling of unknown cause.

Tests you may have

  • blood tests for inflammation, uric acid and infection
  • fluid taken from the joint with a needle to check for infection or crystals
  • X-ray or ultrasound
  • tests for infections that can trigger reactive arthritis

If you already have arthritis

Not every swollen joint is a flare. If one joint is much more swollen and painful than your usual flares, or you feel unwell or feverish, seek urgent advice, especially if you take steroids, DMARDs or biologics, which can hide some signs of infection. Do not stop your medicines without advice, but tell the doctor what you take.

Keeping a record

If swelling comes and goes, take photos and note the date, which joint, any triggers and how long it lasted. This helps your GP or rheumatologist work out the cause.

Most sudden joint swelling turns out to have a treatable cause. Getting checked quickly means you get the right treatment sooner and, for infections, protects the joint from lasting damage.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a swollen joint with a high temperature, shivering or feeling very unwell, especially if you have a joint replacement, diabetes or take immune-suppressing medicines
  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
